R0055.title: Unauthorized Discount Purchase
R0055.definition: Zero-price or below-cost purchases resulting from business logic errors or misconfigured prices and coupons.
R0055.description: This attack may be discovered accidentally, but is more likely the result of an attacker probing at scale through automated bulk cart additions, modifying submitted amounts or quantities, or collecting and stacking coupons. After discovering a vulnerability, attackers typically exploit it while simultaneously publicizing it to achieve safety in numbers and conceal their identity, causing greater losses to the platform or merchant.
R0055.influence: Causes significant financial losses to the platform and merchants.

references.title: Financial Weekly: Over 4 Million Financial Black-Grey Market Practitioners in China

observables: The same account or device bulk-adds items to the cart in a short window and places orders at an abnormally low or zero price
Order amounts, quantities, and coupon-stacking combinations deviate from the normal distribution and concentrate on triggering price vulnerabilities
Orders exploiting the vulnerability spike explosively within a short window alongside external propagation (the vulnerability is made public)
The amount actually paid is inverted against the product cost, with a large number of zero or near-zero price orders

R0055-001.title: Coupon Restriction Bypass
R0055-001.definition: Restricted coupons are claimed or used outside their claim or usage restrictions for arbitrage.
R0055-001.description: Two scenarios: first, non-public coupons, coupons claimable under specific conditions, or coupons issued to specific groups are claimed without meeting the restrictions; second, coupons restricted to specific usage scenarios or conditions are used outside those restrictions. Restrictions include: specific time windows, specific user groups, specific product pairings, specific price thresholds, coupon stacking limits, and more.
R0055-001.influence: Exploits platform marketing activity benefits, causing financial losses to the platform.

references.title: OWASP Automated Threat: OAT002 Token Cracking

observables: Non-public or targeted coupons are claimed in bulk by non-target users, with anomalous claim sources
Coupon stacking breaches the rule ceiling, with a single order showing an abnormally high discount ratio
The coupon-claim endpoint shows high-frequency requests with enumeration or token-cracking characteristics and a spike in failure rate
Scenario-restricted coupons are used on non-designated products or time windows, with usage distribution crossing boundaries

R0055-002.title: Unlimited Coupon Claiming
R0055-002.definition: Attackers bypass coupon claim-count, eligibility, or campaign inventory limits to repeatedly claim coupons that should be restricted.
R0055-002.description:
Unlimited coupon claiming usually occurs when the coupon-claim endpoint relies only on client-side state, a single account identifier, or front-end campaign rules. Attackers use multiple accounts, virtual mobile numbers, forged device fingerprints, API replay, or parameter tampering to repeatedly claim new-user coupons, discount coupons, consumption vouchers, and other promotional benefits.

Unlike coupon code enumeration, the core issue is not guessing coupon codes, but bypassing checks for who may claim, how many times they may claim, and whether campaign inventory remains available. At scale, this drains marketing budgets and turns the abuse into direct financial loss through underpriced orders, coupon resale, or fake transactions.
R0055-002.influence: Marketing coupon inventory and subsidy budgets are consumed in bulk, legitimate users cannot claim benefits, and the platform's order pricing is abnormally depressed while subsidy losses increase.

references.title: Business Logic Security Cheat Sheet - OWASP Cheat Sheet Series
BLA1:2025 - Action Limit Overrun - OWASP Top 10 for Business Logic Abuse
Examples of business logic vulnerabilities - PortSwigger Web Security Academy

observables: The same device cluster, phone-number segment, or shipping address repeatedly claims the same campaign coupon in a short window
The coupon-claim endpoint receives replayed or slightly modified requests, with successful claims exceeding campaign limits
Coupon inventory is depleted quickly while redeemed users show very low retention, repurchase, and authentic browsing behavior
Claiming accounts share device fingerprints, proxy IPs, payment accounts, shipping addresses, or other linkage signals

R0055-003.title: Repeated First-Order Reward Claiming
R0055-003.definition: Attackers forge or repeatedly construct new-user, first-order, or first-purchase eligibility to claim first-order discounts, red packets, or referral rewards multiple times.
R0055-003.description:
Repeated first-order reward claiming abuses eligibility for first-order discounts, first-purchase subsidies, new-user coupons, and referral rewards. Attackers use bulk registration, virtual mobile numbers, identity misuse, forged device environments, or replayed referral flows so that the same group is repeatedly recognized as new users or first-order users.

This turns subsidies intended for real acquisition into underpriced orders or cashable rewards. Compared with general marketing campaign cheating, it focuses on failures in transaction-side checks for first-order eligibility, first-order pricing, and first-order reward settlement, and often appears together with fake transactions, proxy ordering, and resale cash-out.
R0055-003.influence: First-order subsidies, acquisition rewards, and new-user benefits are repeatedly extracted, customer acquisition cost is distorted, legitimate new-user benefits are crowded out, and abnormal low-price orders and fake growth data are produced.

references.title: Targeting Telecom and Online Fraud: Criminals Exploit Loopholes in the E-Commerce Economy

observables: Newly registered accounts complete a first order and then immediately become inactive, with no authentic repurchase or browsing path
First-order transactions are highly clustered by device fingerprint, shipping address, payment account, or referral relationship
The same inviter or account cluster repeatedly triggers new-user coupons, first-order discounts, and referral rewards
After first-order rewards are redeemed, goods are quickly resold, refunded, or routed to a small set of linked shipping addresses

R0055-004.title: Payment Amount Tampering
R0055-004.definition: Attackers tamper with order amounts, item quantities, discount amounts, or payment parameters so the actual payment is lower than the amount due.
R0055-004.description:
Payment amount tampering often occurs when server-side consistency checks are missing across order creation, discount calculation, payment confirmation, or callback processing. Attackers use traffic interception, API replay, request-parameter modification, negative quantities, or forged discount fields to submit orders at a low, zero, or even negative amount.

The core issue is that price and payment status depend on client-provided parameters or unsigned fields, while the server does not recalculate product prices, inventory quantities, discount rules, and the amount returned by the payment provider. At scale, this directly causes revenue loss and contaminates transaction, inventory, and finance reconciliation data.
R0055-004.influence: Goods or services are completed below the payable amount, causing direct revenue loss for the platform and merchants while polluting payment, inventory, finance reconciliation, and after-sales workflows.

references.title: Test Payment Functionality - OWASP Web Security Testing Guide

observables: The order payable amount, payment-provider paid amount, and product price snapshot are inconsistent
Amount, quantity, discount, or payment-status fields in checkout requests are modified and the transaction still completes
The same account or device repeatedly submits zero-price, negative, or clearly below-cost orders
The payment callback amount differs from the local order amount, but the order status is still marked as paid
